extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of social science, history, and religion
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-form, historical-sociological examination of the character and influence of religion in the United States, outlining the observable dimensions one should examine to judge religion's social and moral impact. Intended as guidance for forming an overall judgment about how religion shapes conduct, institutions, and imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply and use of external ministrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the external ministrations of religion are supplied to the people and used by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for churches 'everywhere, and everywhere equally' (cities, country, North, South, West), missionary societies supplying ministers in new settlements and mining camps, ratios such as 'a church for every thousand inhabitants' in some towns, and growth of churches as an indication of prosperity. Note denominational rivalry and the maintenance of weak churches from pride rather than need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church attendance / habit of church-going
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevalence of the habit of attending church (e.g., proportion who go to church at least once every Sunday).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reports that in many towns possibly half the native population attended weekly, while attendance is much less in the great cities. Compare attendance trends over time and between urban and rural areas; watch for regional exceptions (e.g., California).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observance of the Sabbath (Sunday practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strictness or laxity of Sunday observance as a test of religious influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine laws and customs forbidding labour and amusement on Sunday (historical statutes cited), whether shops or ordinary work are done, availability of Sunday trains, and whether museums, libraries, and theatres are open. Note that formal laws may be obsolete while supported to the extent they restrict ordinary traffic and labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest in theological questions and knowledge of Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which theological debate, scriptural knowledge, and doctrinal awareness engage the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess changes over time—e.g., declining knowledge of Scripture, less keen interest than in earlier New England days—but also note denominational differences and the continued publication and readership of theological articles in leading reviews and magazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of pulpit teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether sermons are metaphysical/doctrinal or expository/practical and hortatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe tendencies across denominations: many moving toward expository or practical sermons; Southern Presbyterians more doctrinal and conservative; track whether sermons avoid or engage major theological questions (authority of Scripture, science vs. Bible, immortality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of scepticism, unbelief, or agnosticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevalence and social penetration of sceptical or unbelieving views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider statistics and anecdotal evidence about church membership trends, the presence of agnostic circles and secularist lectures in cities, and whether scepticism is increasing among different social strata; the author notes it is difficult for any observer to answer definitively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance and latitude for doctrinal divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which churches permit divergence from traditional formularies and how common prosecutions for heresy are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for loosened bonds of subscription, rarity of heresy prosecutions, public sympathy for accused ministers, and differences by denomination and region (South vs. North); compare ecclesiastical latitude with legal decisions (e.g., 'Essays and Reviews' effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revivalism and emotionalism (camp-meetings etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propensity for revivalist forms of religion and external demonstrations of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify presence and character of camp-meetings, emotional preaching, and their impact—often powerful but transient—especially among humbler classes and in evangelizing frontier districts; note regional persistence (e.g., South) and trends toward these gatherings becoming social outings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social functions of the congregation
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of congregations as centres of social, literary, recreative, philanthropic, and youth activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how churches host supplementary societies, 'sociables', YMCA-type activities, and provide social mixing across classes; evaluate their role in keeping young people engaged and forming acquaintances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion's contribution to philanthropic and benevolent works
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which religious motive and organization underpin charitable giving and personal effort in beneficence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure sums collected relative to national wealth, the amount of personal interest and volunteer effort, and ecumenical cooperation across Protestants and often Catholics in benevolent work; consider how much philanthropy would persist absent religious motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion's influence on moral conduct and ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which religious belief governs conduct—veracity, temperance, domestic purity, tenderness to children, kindness—and the general ethical standard of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare native-born and foreign-born crime levels (with caution), examine indicators like honesty, temperance, domestic behavior, and consider whether religious teaching (even if less dogmatic) remains the primary source of duty and conduct. Note regional variations and cautions about interpreting divorce statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion's effect on imagination and cultural life
rubrics_metrics.description: How far religion 'touches and gilds the imagination' of the people and enriches cultural/spiritual life beyond mere external forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether religion governs merely externals (buildings, revenues) or penetrates belief and conscience; compare to historical analogies (e.g., Roman temples) and seek evidence that religion moulds minds and redeems lives from commonness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical and demographic indicators (membership, communicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measures such as number of church members or communicants relative to population and trends across censuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ church censuses and membership ratios (e.g., communicants rising from 1 in 14½ in 1800 to 1 in 5 in 1880; 1906 census figures) but interpret cautiously alongside attendance, urban/rural differences, and possible under/over-representation.
